name: Geological CO2 storage in saline aquifers
applications: permanent storage of captured CO2 from industry, power and gas processing
principle: Captured CO2 is compressed to a dense phase, piped or shipped to an injection site and injected through wells into a porous rock formation filled with salt water, below an impermeable caprock. The CO2 is trapped under the seal, dissolves in the brine and, over long periods, can mineralise. Injection raises reservoir pressure, so capacity is limited by the pressure that the rock and caprock can tolerate; operators manage it with well placement, completion design and sometimes brine production. Monitoring wells and surveys track the plume.

performance.metric: storage capacity gain from lateral pressure redistribution by brine production, Natuna D-Alpha (simulation)
performance.basis: thick carbonate aquifer; high-rate brine production; multi-depth injection alone gave 13%, both together 44% with storage efficiency 0.58%

source.note: Nirwana et al., Optimizing CO2 Storage in Saline Aquifers through Pressure Redistribution in Natuna D-Alpha Field, SCOG 49(3): 53-66, 2026 (LEMIGAS SCOG, CC BY-SA 4.0)

performance.metric: increase in stored CO2 from completion redesign, SK gas field aquifer (simulation)
performance.basis: 120-year simulation with plume confined to the aquifer zone in most cases; mineral trapping a minor share

source.note: Iskandar et al., Optimized CO2 storage strategies for plume containment and mineral trapping in the SK gas field aquifer, SCOG 49(2): 173-201, 2026 (LEMIGAS SCOG, CC BY-SA 4.0)

performance.metric: pore pressure rise and remaining margin to fracture pressure, sandstone at 1,200 m (simulation)
performance.basis: pore pressure 11.8 to 15.8 MPa against 19.0 MPa fracture pressure, safety ratio 1.20; 10 years injection plus 500 years monitoring

source.note: Fitria et al., Impact of CO2-Induced Geochemical Alteration on the Mechanical Integrity of Reservoir and Caprock in Saline Aquifers, SCOG 49(3): 607-645, 2026 (LEMIGAS SCOG, CC BY-SA 4.0)

performance.metric: Upper Baturaja candidate reservoir depth and porosity (screening)
performance.basis: porosity 20-25%, dominated by secondary porosity; Kandanghaur-Gantar High, West Java; literature-based pre-feasibility

source.note: Musakti et al., Feasibility of Upper Baturaja Interval as a Carbon Storage Reservoir in Kandanghaur-Gantar High, SCOG 49(3): 299-314, 2026 (LEMIGAS SCOG, CC BY-SA 4.0)

performance.metric: net reservoir permeability of the Upper Baturaja interval, Kandanghaur-Gantar High (well-log derived)
performance.basis: Pertamina EP internal petrophysical analysis of more than 40 wells gave 50-70 mD with 14-17% effective porosity; Table 3 screening lists 20-60 mD within Net Reservoir; measured well data, not an injectivity test

source.note: Musakti et al., Feasibility of Upper Baturaja Interval as a Carbon Storage Reservoir in Kandanghaur-Gantar High, SCOG 49(3): 299-314, 2026 (LEMIGAS SCOG, CC BY-SA 4.0), section 3.3 and Table 3

performance.metric: theoretical volumetric CO2 storage capacity across Kandanghaur-Gantar High fields (screening)
performance.basis: volumetric MCO2/HCPV method; ABG field gas and oil columns 25.96 and 1.5 million tonnes at RF 60% and 10% and CO2 density 383.16 kg/m3; MCO2/HCPV 0.23 and 0.038 million tonnes per million m3 of hydrocarbon pore volume; classed theoretical on the techno-economic resource pyramid; Table 2 total 34.48 million tonnes

source.note: Musakti et al., Feasibility of Upper Baturaja Interval as a Carbon Storage Reservoir in Kandanghaur-Gantar High, SCOG 49(3): 299-314, 2026 (LEMIGAS SCOG, CC BY-SA 4.0), section 3.6 and Table 2
IEA ETP Clean Energy Technology Guide, dataset of 24 July 2026, 2025 assessment (IEA 1-11 scale): 'CO2 storage in saline formation' 9

advantages: Large storage potential and wide geographic spread
Pressure management can raise safe capacity substantially in simulations
Indonesian studies exist for Natuna, Jatibarang and gas-field aquifers
limitations: Pressure build-up near injectors limits capacity
Figures here are simulation or screening results, not field performance
Long-term geochemical and mechanical integrity must be shown
notes: Southeast Asian figures on this card are from 2026 LEMIGAS studies using simulation or literature screening. They are not measured results from operating projects.

gaps.item: cost of transport and storage in USD per tonne CO2 with dollar year

reference_plants.name: Sleipner CO2 storage, Utsira Formation, Norwegian North Sea (Equinor)
reference_plants.capacity: about 1 Mt CO2/yr injected into a deep saline formation since 1996; more than 20 Mt stored; injection cost about USD 17/t (storage only); zero leakage detected across 28+ years of monitoring

source.note: MIT Sleipner project page (USD 17/t injection, 15.5 Mt to 2015); ResearchGate review (over 20 Mt stored since 1996); read 2026-10-28

reference_plants.name: Northern Lights CO2 transport and storage, Norway (Equinor/Shell/TotalEnergies)
reference_plants.capacity: world's first merchant CO2 transport and storage: Phase 1 up to 1.5 Mtpa (operational 2024, first injection August 2025); March 2025 FID on a USD 714 m expansion for 900 kt/yr biogenic CO2 over 15 years; Phase 2 to lift capacity to at least 5 Mtpa from 2028

source.note: Equinor Northern Lights page (1.5 Mtpa, expansion to min 5 Mtpa); ogj 27 Mar 2025 (USD 714 m FID); TotalEnergies notice 25 Aug 2025 (first CO2 storage); read 2026-10-28

costs.unit: USD/t CO2 (Sleipner injection/storage only); Northern Lights Phase 2 expansion: USD 714 m capex for 900 kt/yr over 15 years
costs.basis: Sleipner injection cost about USD 17/t CO2 (MIT project page, storage component only; dollar year not stated, page read 2026-10-28); Northern Lights Phase 2 expansion FID USD 714 m for 900,000 t/yr of biogenic CO2 over 15 years (OGJ, 27 Mar 2025) - implying about USD 53/t annualised capex; full-chain transport-plus-storage costs remain project-specific

source.note: MIT Sleipner page; OGJ 27 Mar 2025 for the Northern Lights expansion
